notes:
**Windows** — run `ruze_0.0.26_x64-setup.exe`.
**Linux** — `flatpak install ruze-0.0.26.flatpak`, then `flatpak run com.ruze.chat`.
**Android** — sideload `ruze-0.0.26.apk`. arm64 devices, Android 8.0 or newer.

---

### Added

- **Read a QR code off your own screen.** A phone joins a server by pointing
  its camera at an invite. A desktop has no camera pointed at anything — but
  the code is usually already on the screen, in a browser or in whatever the
  person who sent it is using. So there is a lens: a small window with a hole
  in the middle that you drag over the code and press Read. It is offered
  wherever a phone offers its camera — the first-run screen and Add a server —
  and pasting the ticket is still there underneath.

  The middle of the lens is genuinely see-through: the window is transparent,
  so what you see through it is what gets read, and nothing has to be hidden
  and redrawn to take the picture. If the code turns out to be just outside the
  hole, the whole screen is searched before giving up — lining a window up by
  eye is approximate, and finding it anyway beats being told to try again.

- **An overlay that names whoever is talking, over the game.** A small
  transparent window, above everything else, listing the people in your voice
  channel — because the moment you want to know who is speaking is the moment
  you are looking at something that is not Ruze.

  It cannot be clicked. The window ignores the mouse outright, so every click
  goes through it to whatever is behind, and it never takes the keyboard away
  from what you are playing. That also means nothing in it is a control: it is
  names, a green dot for a live voice, and a mark for anyone on mute.

  Two ways to have it, in Settings → Overlay. It can appear as somebody starts
  talking and go when the room falls quiet — the default, because a list of
  silent names parked over a corner is something you stop seeing and then
  resent — or stay for the whole call. A name lingers a second and a half past
  the last sound either way: speech has gaps in it, and a label that flickers
  on every syllable is worse than no label.

  Pick which corner it sits in, and a shortcut that shows and hides it without
  leaving the game. The shortcut is registered across the whole machine, so it
  is taken away from every other program while Ruze is running — which is why
  it is one combination, chosen by you, and can be set to none at all. If the
  system will not give it to us, the settings panel says so rather than
  leaving you with a key that quietly does nothing.

  Desktop only. A phone has nowhere to put a window over a game.

- **Push to talk, on a key or a mouse button.** Settings → Push to talk. Your
  microphone stays shut until you hold it and shuts again the moment you let
  go, and it reaches Ruze over a full-screen game.

  The mouse is the better half of this, and on Windows it is the one to use:
  the side buttons and the wheel are all offered, and they are *watched* rather
  than taken, so the button goes on doing whatever it already did — bind the
  thumb button and it still goes back in a browser. Left and right are not
  offered, since you would need them to change your mind.

  A key combination has to have a modifier in it, and that is worth saying
  plainly: a shortcut is registered with the system rather than watched for, so
  while Ruze holds one nothing else on the machine sees it. Bind a bare V and
  you stop being able to type the letter V.

  Mouse buttons are Windows-only for now. It needs a low-level hook, and the
  Linux build is a Flatpak — the sandbox exists precisely to stop an
  application watching every input event on the desktop, and under Wayland
  there is no interface for it at any permission level.

  Turning it on shuts the microphone at once and turning it off opens it again,
  so the setting and the microphone cannot disagree — and the key cannot be
  turned on without one, which would shut the microphone with nothing to open
  it.

- **A list of every key that does something**, from the keyboard button in the
  title bar, left of the window controls. It is in two halves, because the
  difference matters: the shortcuts you chose, which work while you are looking
  at a game, and the ones that only work while Ruze is in front. The chosen
  ones are read from the settings, so the list cannot go on claiming a
  combination you have changed.

  Ctrl+F is new alongside it, and opens the search over whatever conversation
  is on screen. It is claimed from the webview's own find bar deliberately:
  that one searches the messages that happen to be rendered, and answering
  "not found" about something that was definitely said is worse than not having
  the key.

- **Search.** A magnifier in the channel header and at the top of every
  conversation. Type words, get the messages that have all of them — case
  ignored, order ignored, and the names of attached files count as text, so
  the spreadsheet somebody sent you is as findable as the sentence about it.
  A channel search can widen to the whole server, and a conversation search to
  all of them.

  It runs entirely on this machine, over the history already on this disk, and
  works with nothing connected — which is the thing a chat app with a server
  in the middle cannot do. There is no index: the entries are read newest-first
  and the walk stops as soon as it has a page of results, so a common word
  costs a handful of reads. A private channel you hold no key to has no
  matches, because there is nothing there this device can read.

- **Admins.** Server settings now lists everyone in the server and lets the
  owner appoint any of them. An admin invites people, answers the door for an
  invite, makes channels, renames the server and removes members — everything
  running a server is — without owning it. What stays with the owner is who
  else runs it: an admin cannot appoint another admin, remove one, or hand the
  server on.

  It works because what an admin signs carries the owner's grant with it: the
  owner-signed admission that made them an admin, attached to every admission
  and invite they issue, so anyone reading one can check the authority behind
  it without asking anybody. Exactly one level deep, which is what stops it
  being the chain of delegation this deliberately is not.

  Taking somebody's admin back stops them letting anyone else in, and leaves
  everyone they already let in exactly where they are — a grant is judged by
  whether it stood when the thing was issued, not by whether it stands now. The
  alternative, and the reason admins did not exist until now, was that
  withdrawing one quietly evicted everybody who had come in through them.

  Removals also count from more devices than they used to: they were honoured
  only from the machine the server was founded on, so an owner's second device
  could remove somebody and nobody else would agree. Now any device of the
  owner's account, and any admin's, is heard.

- **Handing a server over.** The owner can make somebody else the owner, from
  the same list. They get every decision, including whether you keep any; you
  stay on as an admin, so handing over a gated server does not lock you out of
  it. Only the new owner can hand it back — which is why it is the one action
  here that asks you to type the server's name before it will happen.

- **Your account, in a file.** Settings → Account backup writes everything
  that makes up an account to one encrypted file: the 24 words, your name and
  picture, every server you are in, and every friendship. Restoring it on
  another machine makes that machine you, back in all of it.

  The words on their own were never a backup. They restore who you are and
  nothing you had — a server is a key this device holds, a friend is two more,
  and none of them are derived from the phrase — so someone who lost their only
  machine arrived on the new one as themselves, in nothing, knowing nobody.
  Pairing already carried all four things between two live devices; this is the
  same handover with a file where the second device would be, for the case
  where there is no second device left to ask.

  It is encrypted, and not optionally: whoever opens that file is you,
  everywhere, and there is no taking it back. So it takes a passphrase,
  stretched with Argon2id so that guessing at it costs memory rather than
  being free. Nothing outside the encrypted part says whose account it is —
  not the name, not the account id — because a file that names you is a file
  that links you whether or not anyone ever opens it.

  Desktop only. Writing a file needs somewhere to put it, and a phone's answer
  to carrying an account is to pair with another device.

### Changed

- **Settings fill the window.** They were a dialog floating over the
  conversation, which is right for something you answer and wrong for
  somewhere you go — and at 45rem across, half of every panel was a column of
  empty space. It now takes the whole window, below the title bar and no
  further, so the window can still be moved and closed while you are in there.
  What is written on the screen is still held to a readable width; the screen
  is what fills.

- **"See what changed" goes there.** The bar announcing a new version named
  Settings → Updates and left you to find it. It is a link now, and it opens
  settings on that section.

- **The release list shows the five most recent.** It was every release the
  API would hand over, which is a scroll through history to reach the one you
  are being offered. The rest is on the releases page, and the list says so.

### Fixed

- **A device belongs to one person at a time.** A phone or a second machine
  that was paired to your account and then started an account of its own left
  its old member entry behind in every server — leaving a server keeps that
  entry on purpose, and nothing withdraws it afterwards. Both claims stay
  permanently valid, so that one device counted as two people: it was listed
  among the devices of whoever it used to be, a new member joining on it could
  fail to appear in the member list at all, anything it sent was attributed to
  the wrong person, and inside a server whose owner it had been paired to it
  kept an owner device's powers. A device is now whoever it most recently said
  it is.

- **Starting a new account no longer gives away somebody else's server.**
  Servers you own follow you onto a new account, which is right when the
  account is yours alone — and was being applied by any device that merely
  belonged to that account. A paired phone starting a fresh account rewrote the
  server's owner to name it, signed by a device the account had vouched for, so
  every member accepted the handover and the person who made the server stopped
  owning it. A server now moves only when the device changing account is the
  last one that account has in it.

- **Withdrawn invites leave the list.** They stayed on screen, greyed out, as a
  record of a decision already taken. The invite itself has to stay in the
  server — being readable is what makes it turn people away rather than
  puzzle them — but it is no longer something to look at.

- **Your status is the same in every window.** Setting yourself to Busy in one
  window left the other still saying Online. Nothing announced it: choosing a
  status told the network and the tray, and no window at all — so each of them
  sat on whatever it had read when it opened. Going idle now says so too,
  rather than only the window with the timer in it knowing.

- **Attachments arrive in the friends window and in a popped-out
  conversation.** A picture in either used to sit at nought per cent forever:
  those windows were not listening for the transfer they had started. It only
  became visible when conversations learned to carry files, and it affected
  every one of them.

- **Settings can be opened, and browsed, on a phone.** Two faults, one after
  the other. The floating profile card lay across the whole foot of a narrow
  window, and the settings button is at the foot of the server rail — so on a
  phone there was nothing there to press. Once in, the list of sections was
  hidden at that width and the search box was the only way through: reaching
  Storage meant guessing the word for it. The card now sits beside the rail as
  it does on a desktop, and the sections become a row that scrolls sideways.

- **The initials on a server badge can be read.** Each server takes a colour
  from its id and writes its initials on it in white — but a hue is not a
  brightness, and half the wheel came out bright enough that white on it was
  about 2.8:1. Those badges are in the rail, the title bar and on a friend's
  card. The colour now darkens as far as that particular hue needs and no
  further, so the blues are exactly as they were and the yellows and greens
  are legible. The green Join button in a voice channel and four text links
  that were drawn in the button colour rather than the text one are fixed the
  same way.

- **Destructive buttons can be read.** Disconnect, Leave, Delete, Remove and
  eight others are white on the red this app draws errors in, which as a fill
  measures about 3.4:1 — under the line, and on the buttons you least want
  somebody to misread. They take a darker red now; the errors and outlines
  keep the bright one.

- **The first screen fits its card.** With no servers yet, the name and the
  tagline shared a line with your profile row, which left the sentence about
  a hundred pixels wide and broken into five lines down the left edge.

- **The member list opens in a small window.** Below the width that fits a
  conversation and a third column side by side, the Members button went grey
  and there was no way to see who was in the channel until the window was made
  bigger. A narrow window has always opened the list over the conversation
  instead; a cramped desktop one now does the same. Two ways of showing it,
  one button that always works.
